summary: Marlene Mhangami opens with GitHub Octoverse 2025 statistics showing ~1 billion commits—the platform's most active year—and 2026 projections of ~275 million weekly commits extrapolating to ~14 billion annually. She raises whether code volume correlates with real productivity, citing a Stanford study of 120,000 developers showing clean codebases amplify AI gains while unchecked AI amplifies entropy. A case study showed PR volume increased but code quality dropped and rework grew, yielding ~1% effective output improvement. She advocates standardized practices: test coverage, type coverage, documentation, and modularity. She introduces TDD's red-green-refactor cycle (referencing Simon Willison's blog), acknowledging DHH's 2014 critique and recommending Ian Cooper's behavior-driven TDD talk. The core problem: AI-generated tests can be self-affirming—unit suites go green but system behavior isn't validated. Her solution is Playwright (Microsoft's open-source E2E browser testing framework). With AI agents, red and green phases become fast; developers focus on refactoring. Connection options include the Playwright MCP server, CLI tool, or Playwright agents (planner, generator, healer). The live demo adds search/filter features to a Tailspin Toys app using GitHub Copilot CLI with Work IQ to pull a feature-request email, then writes failing Playwright tests first. In the demo continuation, the Playwright MCP server runs functionality tests live—opening the correct page, typing search inputs (finding Furby and Simon correctly), clicking category filter buttons, and validating price range filters—all without manual keyboard input. After tests pass, the workflow moves to refactoring. Best practices include adding Playwright screenshots to PRs, running in headless mode for background execution, committing code before the agent fixes tests, and generating one test per feature. In Q&A, she recommends Playwright agents with specialized agent.md instructions for state management-heavy apps, or directly testing APIs as an alternative, confirms Playwright can test mobile and desktop screen sizes, and notes it is browser-based only for now.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: GitHub Octoverse stats and AI productivity question
sections.summary: Mhangami introduces herself as a senior developer advocate at Microsoft and GitHub in Core AI. She presents GitHub Octoverse 2025 stats: ~1 billion commits, the most active year ever. In 2026, ~275 million weekly commits extrapolate to ~14 billion annually. A growing share is AI co-authored. She asks whether this volume correlates with real productivity.

sections.title: Clean codebase amplifies AI gains
sections.summary: Citing a Stanford study of 120,000 developers, she shows that clean codebases amplify AI productivity while unchecked AI amplifies entropy. A case study showed increased PRs but decreased code quality and more rework, yielding ~1% effective output gain. She advocates standardizing practices: test coverage, type coverage, documentation, modularity.

sections.title: TDD Red-Green-Refactor and criticisms
sections.summary: Introduces red-green TDD (referencing Simon Willison): write a failing test, get it to pass quickly, then refactor for quality. Acknowledges criticisms—DHH's 2014 post on over-focus on unit tests, testing implementation details. Recommends Ian Cooper's talk 'TDD where it all went wrong' and behavior-driven testing against stable contracts.

sections.title: Self-affirming AI tests and Playwright solution
sections.summary: AI-generated tests can be self-affirming: unit suites pass green but system behavior isn't validated. Introduces Playwright (Microsoft open-source E2E browser testing) for functional testing. With AI, red and green phases become fast; developers focus on refactoring. Connection options: Playwright MCP server, CLI tool, or Playwright agents (planner, generator, healer).

sections.title: Live demo: Tailspin Toys search and filter features
sections.summary: Demo scenario: developer at Tailspin Toys receives an email requesting search bar (text + Azure AI search) and sidebar filters (category, price). Uses GitHub Copilot CLI with Work IQ to pull the email into the terminal. Asks Copilot to implement using red-green TDD, starting with failing Playwright tests. The agent first examines the codebase before proceeding.

sections.title: Demo continuation: Playwright tests run live and best practices
sections.summary: The Playwright MCP server runs functionality tests live: opening the correct page, typing search inputs (Furby and Simon found correctly), clicking category filter buttons, and validating price range filters—all without manual keyboard input. All tests pass, confirming the app works as expected. After tests pass, the workflow moves to refactoring. Best practices shared: add Playwright screenshots to PRs, use headless mode for background execution, commit code before the agent fixes tests to preserve history, and generate one test per feature.

sections.title: Q&A: State management, screen sizes, and browser-only limitation
sections.summary: For complex state management, recommends Playwright agents with specialized agent.md instructions, or directly testing APIs as an alternative. Confirms Playwright can test both mobile and desktop screen sizes. Notes Playwright is currently browser-based only. Speaker mentions slides are available online but forgot to include the GitHub repo link.
